name: Lateral approach to the humeral shaft
aliases: lateral paratricipital approach to the humerus
corridor: Lateral interval along the lateral intermuscular septum, identifying the radial nerve and following it to expose the distal two-thirds of the humerus

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral with the arm supported and the whole humerus from deltoid insertion to lateral epicondyle accessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the deltoid insertion, the lateral epicondyle, and the lateral intermuscular septum.

incision.text: Follow a line from the deltoid insertion to the lateral epicondyle, extending proximally along the anterior or posterior deltoid margin as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the deep fascia posterior to the lateral intermuscular septum and enter the posterior compartment between triceps and the septum, developing the plane from distal to proximal.

deep_interval.text: Identify the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and follow it proximally to the radial nerve, find the radial nerve in the fat adjacent to triceps in the middle third, and distally follow it between brachialis and brachioradialis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, deep fascia, the lateral intermuscular septum, the radial nerve, and the humeral shaft.

structures_at_risk.text: The radial nerve, crossing from posterior to anterior across the mid-humerus, is the principal structure at risk and must be identified and protected.

danger_zones.text: The mid-humeral segment where the radial nerve crosses is the danger zone; identify the nerve before working on bone there.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the radial nerve gently and avoid stretching it while exposing the underlying bone.

exposure.text: Exposes the distal two-thirds of the humerus and can extend proximally to the proximal humerus.

limitations.text: Proximal extension along the deltopectoral interval does not reach the proximal radial nerve, and posterior deltoid extension gives more limited bone exposure.

indications.text: Indicated for plating of distal-two-thirds humeral shaft fractures where radial nerve control is required.

closure.text: Ensure the radial nerve lies in a healthy soft-tissue bed and close the incision in layers in the standard manner.

complications.text: The main complication is radial nerve palsy; wound problems may also occur.

procedure_applications.condition: A distal-two-thirds humeral shaft fracture is plated through a lateral exposure with radial nerve control

questions.question: How is the radial nerve first located in the lateral humeral approach?
questions.answer: By finding the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and following it proximally to the radial nerve.

questions.question: Between which muscles is the radial nerve followed distally?
How much of the humerus does the lateral approach expose?
questions.answer: The distal two-thirds, with possible proximal extension.
